questions.question: What does `setTimeout(fn, 0)` actually guarantee?
options: fn runs immediately, before any other code
fn is scheduled to run as a macrotask, only after the current call stack is empty and all pending microtasks have been drained
fn runs exactly 0 milliseconds after the current function returns, ahead of Promises
fn never actually runs if there is other code queued
questions.explanation: A 0ms timeout still places its callback in the macrotask queue, which is only processed after the stack clears and the entire microtask queue is drained.

questions.question: Given `console.log("1"); setTimeout(() => console.log("2"), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("3")); console.log("4");` what is the output order?
questions.explanation: Synchronous logs (1, 4) run first; then the microtask queue (Promise then, logging 3) is fully drained; only then does the macrotask queue run (setTimeout, logging 2).

questions.question: If a microtask callback schedules another microtask while it runs, what happens?
options: The new microtask is deferred until after the next macrotask
The new microtask is also executed before the event loop moves on to the next macrotask, since the microtask queue is drained completely each cycle
It causes an infinite loop error
questions.explanation: The event loop keeps processing microtasks — including ones added during microtask execution — until the microtask queue is completely empty, before touching the next macrotask.

questions.question: Which of the following is processed as a macrotask, not a microtask?
options: A .then() callback on a resolved Promise
An async function's code after an awaited Promise resolves
questions.explanation: setTimeout/setInterval callbacks go to the macrotask (task) queue; Promise continuations and queueMicrotask callbacks go to the microtask queue, which has priority.
